sweep_summary: One title-keyword item for Alyawarr: Goedemans 1998 'Weightless Segments' (Leiden PhD, open access), already held by the project from the umbu1235/kokn1236 checks and now copied to with an Alyawarra excerpt file and a line. It is relevant to Alyawarr word stress but second-hand: sec. 6.2 pp. 154-158 restates Yallop 1977 (C-initial words stressed on syllable 1; vowel- and glide-initial words, disyllables included, on syllable 2; alternating secondaries; App. D VIII p. 248 'stress on the first postconsonantal syllable'). The surface rule confirms the catalog's deciding Yallop 1977 p. 43 quotation. On the classification it refines rather than confirms: the catalog's 'weight' kind follows Gordon 2005's onset-sensitive-weight reading, while Goedemans (pp. 136-137, 168-169) argues explicitly that 'onset sensitivity does not have anything to do with weight' and gives a quantity-insensitive analysis (initial onsetless syllable skipped, ALIGN-FTO over FT-BIN). The empirical conditioning (placement by onset presence) is undisputed; only the theoretical label differs. No new primary stress statement; Yallop 1977 remains the deciding source (Turtle 1977 pp. 48-50, downloaded in our earlier reading, is the other first-hand source and agrees). Nothing left to acquire for this search of works with stress in the title; priority none.

new_statements.quote: Yallop (1977) describes the Alyawarra stress system as follows: disyllabic words can have main stress on the second syllable if they begin with a vowel, else stress falls on the initial syllable (compare the examples in (4) to the corresponding Aranda words). (4) athá 'I (erg.)' kwíya 'girl' iylpá 'ear' kíra 'meat'. Otherwise stress is like in Aranda (cf. 5a), except that words of more than two syllables beginning with a glide also have main stress on the second syllable (cf. 5b). Yallop further notes that words with an initial consonant are far less common than in Aranda. (5) a. ilípa 'axe' párriyka 'fence' apmpírnitjìka 'will cook' ngkwárlilànima place name b. walíymparra 'pelican' yukúntja 'ashes'

new_statements.reading: Main stress on the first syllable that begins with a true consonant: consonant-initial words on syllable 1, vowel-initial and glide-initial (wa-, yu-) words on syllable 2, in disyllables as well as longer words; secondary stress on alternate syllables to the right (p. 136). Goedemans classes this as 'stress on the first postconsonantal syllable' (App. D VIII) and explicitly rejects a weight (moraic-onset) analysis in favour of a quantity-insensitive account with the initial onsetless syllable skipped. This is a second-hand digest of Yallop 1977, not a first-hand statement; it matches the catalog's deciding Yallop p. 43 snippets (a'tha, am'pa, i'lipa, wa'liymparra, yu'kuntja) and the Turtle 1977 (SIL WP A-1 pp. 48-50) scanned already held by the project (vowel- or y-initial words: second syllable; other consonant-initial: first syllable, with listed exceptions).

new_statements.quote: If there is only one vowel sound in a word then it is stressed. rA he, she, it. In Alyawarr the stress is usually on the first vowel after a consonant or consonant cluster. Examples: arrAkert mouth; antEtherrk Centralian Python. If the word begins with a consonant, the stress is on the first syllable. If the word begins with a vowel, the stress is on the second syllable.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (second stress = first postconsonantal syllable) and as Goedemans' digest of Yallop 1977 and the Turtle 1977 SIL WP A-1 scan held held by the project. Adds nothing on secondary stress or weight; is a popular-orthography statement, less detailed than Turtle/Yallop (does not say that y-initial words take second-syllable stress).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Main stress on the first vowel that follows a consonant (or consonant cluster): consonant-initial words are stressed on the first syllable, vowel-initial words on the second syllable; monosyllables are stressed. The dictionary hedges with 'usually'. Stress is said not to be contrastive in the way English permit/PERmit is, though misplaced stress hinders comprehension.
new_statements.exceptions: None listed; the wording 'usually' signals unstated exceptions. No mention of the Yallop/Turtle observation that glide-initial (y-, w-) words pattern with vowel-initial ones.
new_statements.identity_note: The 2019 dictionary describes Alyawarr as written in the IAD community orthography (Central Australian Alyawarr, the Sandover/Utopia region varieties the dictionary covers); it does not name a specific dialect in the Stress section. Turtle 1977 (already held) describes Alyawarra as spoken at Lake Nash/Ammaroo; Yallop 1977 (via Goedemans) the MacDonald Downs variety. All agree on placement.

sources.quote: The most widespread stress rule in Arandic, usually stated: main stress falls on the first vowel that follows a consonant, does not have a simple statement in terms of conventional syllables, but is: stress falls on the second syllable with VC(C) syllables. Henderson (1990) found also that plural and reciprocal morphology is sensitive to whether stems are monosyllabic or disyllabic, but the rule is straightforward only with the VC(C) model.

sources.access_detail: open copy posted by the author (located 2026-09-25); a digital copy (available on request)
sources.quote: In Alyawarra, another Arandic language, stress falls on the initial syllable of words beginning with a [+consonantal] segment (as in (27a)) and on the second syllable of words beginning with a [-consonantal] segment (as in (27b) and (27c)). In other words, stress falls on the initial syllable unless the word begins with a vowel or glide, in which case it falls on the second. Moreover, unlike Western Aranda, main stress can fall on final syllables in bisyllabic words (as is seen be [sic, scanned] some examples in (27b) and (27c)).

Primary stress: first syllable with a [+consonantal] onset; vowel-initial and glide-initial (/y/, /w/) words stress the second syllable, including bisyllables (final stress in ilpá, ingwá, waká), matching the catalog second stress. sources.quote: p. 48: "Contrastive stress is a feature of the Alyawarra word, shown most clearly by the following pair: /'yinpa/ ['yin.b(A)] 'skin' / /yin'pa/ [yin.'bA] 'don't know'. For most words, however, predominant stress patterns are apparent. In words beginning with a vowel or /y/, irrespective of the number of syllables making up the word, stress falls on the second syllable." p. 49: "The relatively few exceptions to the above pattern are listed below:" [ten /y/-initial words with initial stress, e.g. /ya:na/ ['ya.n(A)] 'that', /yilaka/ ['yi.la.k(A)] 'what', /ya:kuta/ ['ya.ku.t(A)] 'bag'] "One word carries even stress on both syllables: /yu:yu:/ ['yo.'yo ~ 'yoo.'yo] 'yes'. In words beginning with any consonant other than /y/ the stress falls on the first syllable, again irrespective of the number of syllables contained in the word." p. 50: "The relatively few exceptions to this rule are as follows:" /wa:lta/ [wal.'dA] 'nulla nulla', /ka:lta/ [kal.'dA] 'hair', /pulurna/ [pu.'lur.ng(A)] 'bird (species)', /tirakara/ [tr.'A.gA.r(A)] 'cockatoo', /mulurai:yira/ [mu.'lu.ra.yi.r(A)] 'witchetty grub (species)'.
sources.note: Vowel-initial branch of the catalog rule (01, 010, 0100..) confirmed exactly: V-initial words stress the second syllable regardless of length (examples up to 7 syllables, e.g. /i:tatari:tatara/ [i.'dA.tA.ri.dA.tA.r(A)] 'willy wag tail'). Adds the consonant-initial branch (initial stress: /mura/ ['mu.r(A)] 'good', /ka:puta/ ['ka.pu.d(A)] 'head', /tyilapatyila/ 'navel'), which the bitstring does not transcribe.
